newsitem.title: UK: Demand for heavy fuel to fall in Europe in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Demand for heavy fuel to fall in Europe in 1997.

text.p: European heavy fuel oil prices may shuffle sideways in the coming months after recent falls which were triggered by dwindling demand from Italy and Portugal, traders and analysts said.
Any such move is likely to be volatile due to low oil stocks, which are over six percent below year-ago levels.
"Our outlook for fuel oil demand is an underlying fall of one percent per year, all other things being equal," said energy analyst Colin Birch of Purvin and Gertz in London.
Low sulphur fuel oil prices have fallen by $20 a tonne to $117 a tonne in Northwest Europe over the past month and supply has piled up across Europe.
Pivotal to this market is the huge Italian state power company ENEL, the world's largest buyer of fuel oil accounting for some 90 percent of Italy's fuel market.
An Italian industry source expected Italian imports of fuel to fall by around 2 million tonnes to 25 million as gas carves out a bigger slice of the energy market.
"That estimate (of 25 million in 1997) was made in October and must be revised but it is still relatively accurate," he said.
Another source saw Italy's consumption of natural gas for power generation rising at a steady 10 percent per year from 1995 to 2000.
He declined to give a precise forecast for 1997 but said 10.0 million tonnes of oil eqivalent went to Italian power stations in 1996, versus 9.4 million in 1995.

Portuguese fuel oil purchases for the first quarter of 1997 will also be sharply lower because of heavy rains and snow this winter which boosted hydro electric output, a source at state company Electricidade de Portugal said.
"Our fuel oil buying in the first quarter will be about equal to this time last year," he said.

Portugal's fuel oil purchases were lower last winter because of record hydro production which took dam levels up to 90 percent of capacity last February. Dam levels this week were at 63 percent but snowfall was heavier this winter, ensuring strong hydro power output for at least the next few months, the source added.
Portugal typically consumes 3-4 million tonnes of high sulphur fuel oil a year. Analysts do not expect regulatory changes this year which will affect imports.
On the supply side, some tightness will emerge as over 200,000 barrels per day (bpd) of northwest European refining capacity closes.
Russian fuel oil exports, however, constitute a wild card.

Exports traditionally fall sharply in winter but some dealers say they think exports this winter may not be as small as in previous years as Russian traders become more sophisticated, and hold back from exporting as much in summer when international prices are low.
Fuel and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov said at the end of last month a fuel oil export tax was being prepared.
"Predicting what is going to happen next in Russia is pretty worthless," one trader said.
Birch predicted a slight widening of the price spread between high and low sulphur fuel oil in 1997.

Although a reduction of allowed levels of sulphur in diesel has led to European refiners buying sweeter crudes, boosting output of low sulphur fuel oil, ongoing moves to curb sulphur emissions mean demand for high sulphur product will dwindle, he said.
And the addition of over half a million barrels per day of high sulphur Iraqi crudes since the U.N. oil-for-food deal reached in December will further depress high sulphur fuel oil prices.
"We see the spread widening a little," he said.
